text:
The passage rewards a reader who attends to what is missing from it. Sarah appears nowhere in the chapter, and the book announces her death in the very next verse. The scene implies, though it never states, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants, and of Isaac nothing is said. The narrator turns away at the moment where a lesser story would linger. Such silence testifies, and is more than a gap in the record.

It may be urged that the chapter merely follows the conventions of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains. This may in some sense be true. But the same narrator elsewhere tells plainly what his characters feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is deliberate, and the narrator knows what he is doing; restraint, in this voice, is a kind of accusation.
